You are BIE's book-understanding section: an expert teacher of Indian Economy for UPSC / State PCS aspirants preparing for UPSC / State PCS.
You read one page of a book chapter with two eyes, the page's native text blocks and the page image, and turn it into a complete,
question-based teacher's understanding. Later BIE sections build the video lessons, the chapter game and the notes only from what you
capture, so anything you miss is missing from the whole course. Your output is internal to BIE: write it in clear English and keep the
book's own terms and spellings.
Course: "3. Money" · subject: Indian Economy · learners: UPSC / State PCS aspirants · exam: UPSC / State PCS · learner language: Hinglish.

Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember. Depth means understanding, not length: lesson narration keeps S2-01's time by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never drop or compress away what the book teaches to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, the book's content is complete. Lesson narration has a time target (S2-01), met by cutting repetition and side-tracks, never book content.
[G-06] BIE is the link between the learner and the book, like a teacher (Navin, 24 October 2026). The book is the base; BIE carries its text, easy or hard, into the learner's mind. Never just read the line out: every book line is opened (what its words mean, why it is so, where it is seen, what follows), at the depth of the level profile.
[G-07] Two layers, like a film (Navin, 24 October 2026). The writer layer (understanding, plan, script) decides what is said and how deep, following the level profile and the book's own level. The presentation layer (director, video blocks, render) is the same skilled quality for every learner, from class 6 to postgraduate; only the detail shown follows the level, never the craft.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.
[S1-11] Where the text layer and the image disagree (garbled symbols, missing words, wrong order), report the disagreement. Trust the image for symbols, layout and diagrams, and the text layer for spelling when it is clean.
[S1-13] A printed typo stays as printed, with the right word after it in square brackets: 'Cartiage [Cartilage]' (Navin, 23 October 2026). The teacher answers use the right word. Never correct the book silently.
[S1-14] One answer, one basis (Navin, 23 October 2026): an answer that would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one with basis 'book' (only what the page states) and one with basis 'outside'.
[S1-15] Open every teachable item for the learner (Navin, 24 October 2026): in unpack, the terms the learner must hold (each with its plain meaning in simple Hindi and one everyday image), a why chain of 1-4 steps that starts from a need or a problem (each step names its basis, book or standard), an example or the place where it is seen, the consequence, the visual verb the video should show, and what the level profile adds. Every teachable item has at least one unpack element; an unpack that only restates the item in other words is empty.
[S1-16] Apply every economics concept in the real world first (Navin, 27 October 2026): in a chapter of the economics family, every definition, cause_effect and process item carries in its unpack a real_world_example: a place (bazaar, kirana shop, mandi, bank, factory, petrol pump, farm), actors (shopkeeper, buyers, farmer, worker, bank, RBI, government), real goods or money (sugar, onion, petrol, salary, loan, EMI), numbers that change (before → after) and at least two steps, each mapped to a link of the concept's mechanism; then the sentence that names the term after the story, and one line on where the learner meets it in real life. The example is economically correct (the mechanism it runs is the concept's) and fits the learner's level (UPSC: the real Indian link, for example repo rate → home-loan EMI, only from the book or a dated source). Navin's example: a kirana shop with 3 packets of sugar at ₹50, buyers 2 → 12, the price ₹65, only 3 can buy: demand-pull inflation.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

How BIE talks to you: every request is a task card (JSON) followed by its source. The card names the unit, its parts with their content type and required questions, the ids of the rules above that apply, the output, the ids you must cover and the context. The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.
For a read_page card:
- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;
  "pNNNN-image" is the page image), with the evidence in "focus". It is a proposal from keywords and patterns, not a verdict: give
  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that
  item's type_note; BIE's code compares every item and sends unexplained differences back to you.
- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "". When the page
    starts with the options of a question printed on the previous page, add one question item for that question (content: "continued
    from the previous page" and what the options answer) and make it their parent.
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a
    table_row; what a label names and what it points to for a diagram_label; all branches for a tree). A printed typo stays as
    printed with the right word after it in square brackets, "Cartiage [Cartilage]" (S1-13); never correct the book silently.
  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.
  - teachable: false only for pure headings and containers whose children carry the content.
  - teacher_understanding: the teacher's questions and answers for this item (S1-06); depth 1 for first questions, 2 and more for
    "why"/"how" on an earlier answer; basis "book" only if the page states it, else "outside"; one answer, one basis: an answer that
    would mix what the book says with an outside explanation becomes two answers, one "book" and one "outside" (S1-14). BIE's code
    checks every teachable item:
    at least two questions, at least one "why" or "how", at least the required questions of its content type, and no answer that only
    repeats its question or the item's words.
  - prerequisites: concrete concepts a student must understand first.
  - exam_importance and exam_note: for this exam.
  - tests_item_ids: for a question, the ids on this page that it tests ([] if they are on other pages).
  - unpack: how a teacher opens this book line for the learner (S1-15; BIE is the link between the learner and the book, never a
    reader of the line). For every teachable item, at the depth of the level profile below:
    terms = the words of the line the learner must own: [{term (as the book spells it), plain_meaning (everyday spoken Hindi in Devanagari
    with the book's English terms in Roman: "tissue", "cell", "epithelium", "muscle", never their textbook Hindi ऊतक, कोशिका, उपकला, मांसपेशी;
    BIE's code sends an item back for a textbook translation. For example "absorptive surface" → "जहाँ चीज़ें अंदर ली जाती हैं"),
    everyday_image (one image from the learner's
    home or body: "आँत खाने के पोषक तत्व सोखती है, जैसे कागज़ पानी")}]; why_chain = the why in steps, starting from a need or a
    problem ("पेट में HCl बनता है, इसलिए अंदर एक lining चाहिए"), each step with its basis: "book" when the page says it, "standard"
    when it is standard textbook knowledge; example_or_place = one example, or the place by a zoom from the organ the learner knows;
    consequence = what follows, and the link to the previous or the next idea of the page; visual_verb = what visibly happens on the
    screen when this is taught ("particles cross the thin layer"); level_extra = what this level adds (the other names, the exam's
    trap, the memory trick) or "". BIE's code checks that every teachable item has at least one unpack element and that every why
    step names its basis; a locked explanation given with the source is reused as it is. A question item or a pure heading leaves
    unpack empty.
  - unpack.real_world_example (S1-16; Navin, 27 October 2026: "economic concepts ko real world mein apply karke samjhao"): in a chapter
    of the economics family, for every definition, cause_effect and process item, the concept APPLIED in an everyday Indian situation
    before it is named: place (bazaar, kirana shop, mandi, bank, factory, petrol pump, farm); actors (shopkeeper, buyers, farmer,
    worker, bank, RBI, government); goods (the real goods or money: sugar, onion, petrol, salary, loan, EMI); numbers (each
    {what, before, after}, written with digits: {"what": "price", "before": "₹50", "after": "₹65"}, {"what": "buyers", "before": "2",
    "after": "12"}); steps (at least two, each {step, mechanism_link}: the story step by step, and the link of the concept's mechanism
    that step shows); term_after (the sentence that names the term only after the story: "isliye ise demand-pull inflation kehte
    hain"); real_life_link (one line on where the learner meets it; UPSC: the real Indian link, for example repo rate → home-loan EMI,
    only from the page or a dated source). The example must be economically correct: the mechanism it runs is the concept's, and the
    numbers move the way the concept says. Navin's example: a kirana shop with 3 packets of sugar at ₹50; buyers 2 → 12; the price
    ₹65; only 3 can buy: demand-pull inflation. BIE's code checks the place, an actor, the goods, a number that changes, two steps with
    their links, term_after and real_life_link. Every other item (another subject family, another type, a question, a heading) leaves
    it empty ("" and []).
- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.
- text_image_disagreements: where the text layer and the image differ.
Reply with the JSON object only.

Level profile: UPSC / State PCS (level_profiles.json; learners: UPSC and State PCS aspirants, often from arts backgrounds, who need understanding more than technical vocabulary).
- Terms: fewer technical terms: only the ones the exam asks, each opened with its plain meaning and an everyday image; a term the exam never asks is explained in words, not named.
- Why: 2 step(s); a two-step why from a need the learner can feel, then its link to daily life, health or governance.
- Where found: the main places, each linked to something the learner already knows (a disease, a food, a news item).
- Exam beats: the PYQ pattern: how this fact has been asked (statement combinations, 'which is correct', odd one out) and the wording that traps.
- Links: daily life, health, the news and earlier chapters of the same paper.

How real teachers open a book line (teacher example bank 2026-10-27.1; use these ways, in your own words):
- One everyday image per shape or function (every term that names a shape, a layer or a job): Chaadar bichhi ho to bistar bacha rehta hai = protective sheet. Cube wala game, har side barabar = cuboidal. Building ka pillar = columnar. Farsh ki tiles = squamous, isliye tessellated bhi kehte hain.
- The word root where it helps (a term whose parts carry its meaning): Epi yaani upar; epithelium yaani upar ki parat. Slender yaani long aur narrow.
- Why starts from a need (every why step): Pet mein HCl banta hai, isliye andar ek lining chahiye jo khud na jale. Cells bahar ki taraf hain, tootne ka chance zyada, isliye regeneration zyada.
- Link to something already known (a new place or a new structure): Peritoneum, jaise lungs ke aas-paas pleura aur heart ke aas-paas pericardium: wahi kaam, pet ke andar.
- Meaning with two or three real examples (an abstract word in the book): Sensory perception yaani pehchanna: thanda lagna, dard hona, pressure mehsoos karna.
- Open the book's adjective (Navin's example) (a book line names a kind of surface, job or place without saying what it is): Book: 'epithelium absorptive aur secretive surfaces par milta hai'. Teacher: absorptive surface yaani jahan cheezein andar li jaati hain, jaise aant khane ke poshak tatva sokhti hai; secretive yaani jahan cells kuch bana kar bahar chhodte hain, jaise glands enzyme ya juice. Aur epithelium wahan kyon? Kyunki ek patli, lagi hui parat hi cheezon ko paar jaane de sakti hai aur bana kar chhod sakti hai.
- Apply it in the real world first, then name it (Navin's sugar shop) (every economics concept (a definition, a cause-and-effect chain, a process): the example runs before the term is named): Ek kirana shop mein chini ke 3 packet hain, ₹50 ka ek. Kal 2 khareedar aaye the, aaj 12 aa gaye; sab ko chini chahiye par packet 3 hi hain. Dukandar daam ₹65 kar deta hai; ab sirf 3 log kharid paate hain, baaki 9 khaali haath. Zyada log, utna hi maal, isliye daam upar. Isliye ise demand-pull inflation kehte hain. Phir book ki definition. Phir: yahi aap Diwali se pehle sabzi mandi mein dekhte hain.

items.content: It includes almost all liquid money available in the economy, including Post Office deposits that are not included in M3.

teacher_understanding.question: What coverage does this continuation attribute to M4?
teacher_understanding.answer: It includes almost all liquid money in the economy and extends beyond M3 to include Post Office deposits.

teacher_understanding.question: What on this page makes clear that M4 is broader than M3?
teacher_understanding.answer: The following equation adds Post Office Savings Bank deposits to M3, while excluding National Savings Certificates.

teacher_understanding.question: Why distinguish liquid money from wealth generally?
teacher_understanding.answer: A person can own valuable assets without being able to use them readily for payments. Liquidity concerns how readily purchasing power becomes available, not simply how valuable an asset is.

prerequisites: money supply as an economy-wide stock
items.exam_note: Do not confuse a broad money aggregate with all wealth or all financial assets.

why_chain.step: To measure purchasing power, distinguish readily usable money from assets that take time to turn into money.
The book's wider aggregate brings in Post Office deposits beyond M3.

unpack.example_or_place: A household comparing money held in a bank and in a Post Office deposit.
unpack.consequence: M4 has wider coverage than M3, but does not include every savings instrument.
unpack.visual_verb: expand the M3 boundary to include Post Office deposits
unpack.level_extra: The pronoun 'It' continues the discussion of M4; 'almost all' is not 'all wealth'.

items.content: M4 = M3 + All Deposits with Post Office Savings Banks (excluding National Savings Certificates)

teacher_understanding.question: How should the equation and its symbols be read?
teacher_understanding.answer: M4 is the monetary aggregate being calculated; M3 is the narrower aggregate used as its base. '=' means equals and '+' means add the eligible Post Office Savings Bank deposits. National Savings Certificates are excluded. All component stocks must be measured in the same monetary unit, such as rupees, for the same date.

teacher_understanding.question: Which explicit qualification limits 'All Deposits'?
teacher_understanding.answer: The parentheses explicitly exclude National Savings Certificates.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a learner apply this without double-counting?
teacher_understanding.answer: Start with M3 once and add only the specified additional deposits. In a hypothetical calculation, M3 of ₹1,000 plus eligible Post Office deposits of ₹200 gives M4 of ₹1,200; an NSC holding is not added.

items.exam_note: High-yield aggregate formula; the NSC exclusion is the key statement trap.

terms.everyday_image: हिसाब बनाते समय एक पर्ची को अलग रख देना।

why_chain.step: A wider money measure needs to cover eligible deposits outside the M3 boundary.
Add Post Office Savings Bank deposits but leave National Savings Certificates outside.

unpack.consequence: An increase in eligible additional deposits, other things equal, widens the gap between M4 and M3.
unpack.visual_verb: add the deposit block and exclude the NSC card
unpack.level_extra: These are aggregate money stocks, not a formula for one person's total wealth.

items.content:
The National Savings Certificate (NSC) is not counted in M4 because:
It is a long-term savings instrument, not readily spendable money.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does the book exclude NSCs from M4?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies an NSC as a long-term savings instrument rather than readily spendable money.

teacher_understanding.question: How does that distinction matter for ordinary purchases?
teacher_understanding.answer: A savings claim can preserve value without functioning like a readily usable payment balance. A shopper cannot ordinarily hand an NSC to a shopkeeper as payment; money must first become available under the instrument's rules.

teacher_understanding.question: What follows for the idea that every Post Office product belongs in M4?
teacher_understanding.answer: That idea is incorrect: this page expressly names an excluded Post Office savings instrument.

items.exam_note: An explicit exception suitable for correct/incorrect statement and odd-one-out questions.

terms.plain_meaning: लंबे समय के लिए बचत रखने का साधन; रोज की खरीदारी वाला पैसा नहीं
terms.everyday_image: बचत का कागज संभालकर रखना, लेकिन दुकान पर उससे सीधे भुगतान न कर पाना।

why_chain.step: A household needs usable money to meet today's expenses, not merely a claim on future savings.
The book treats NSCs as long-term and not readily spendable, so excludes them from M4.

unpack.example_or_place: A household's Post Office savings compared with money available for groceries.
unpack.consequence: Owning an NSC adds to savings but does not make it an included component of M4.
unpack.visual_verb: separate the savings certificate from the spendable-money basket
unpack.level_extra: Do not infer that every long-term deposit is excluded from broad money; remember the specific NSC exclusion.

Find correct statement(s) about “Blockchain Technology” [UPSC-Prelims-2020]
1. It is a public ledger that everyone can inspect, but which no single user controls.
2. Structure and design of blockchain is such that all the data in it are about cryptocurrency only.
3. Applications that use basic features of blockchain can be developed without anybody’s permission.
Answer Codes:
items.type_note: An exam year is not a timeline; these are statements to evaluate, not established facts.

teacher_understanding.question: Which option answers this question?
teacher_understanding.answer: Option d, 1 and 3 only, is the standard answer in the public, permissionless blockchain context used by this question. Statement 2 is incorrect.

teacher_understanding.question: How can a ledger be inspectable without being controlled by one user?
teacher_understanding.answer: In a public blockchain, records are shared across a network and updates follow agreed validation rules. Inspecting a record does not give one participant unilateral power to rewrite the shared history.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is 'cryptocurrency only' the trap?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blockchain is a way to maintain shared records, not a restriction on what those records describe. Applications may record supply-chain movements or verify documents as well as support cryptocurrency.

teacher_understanding.question: How should statement 3 be understood without overgeneralising?
teacher_understanding.answer: Developers can build applications using open, permissionless blockchain features without a central owner's permission. That does not remove legal obligations or mean private and permissioned networks offer unrestricted access.

prerequisites: ledger as a record of transactions
items.exam_note: UPSC 2020 statement-combination question; distinguish the technology from cryptocurrency and public networks from permissioned ones. No printed key.

teacher_understanding.question: Is this the correct combination?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. It accepts statement 1 but omits the correct statement 3.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is omitting statement 3 incorrect here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The question assumes open blockchain features that developers can use without a central owner's permission.

items.exam_note: Incomplete combination.

teacher_understanding.question: Is this combination correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. It includes the false statement 2 and excludes the correct statement 3.

teacher_understanding.question: Why cannot statement 2 be accepted?
teacher_understanding.answer: A blockchain can carry records unrelated to cryptocurrency, such as supply-chain records.

items.exam_note: Reject the cryptocurrency-only restriction.

teacher_understanding.question: Is this option correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. It selects the incorrect statement and omits both correct statements.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is identifying blockchain with cryptocurrency misleading?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cryptocurrency is one application; the shared-record technology can serve other purposes.

items.exam_note: The word 'only' makes statement 2 false.

teacher_understanding.question: Is this the standard answer?
teacher_understanding.answer: Yes, in the public, permissionless blockchain context of this question.

teacher_understanding.question: Why do statements 1 and 3 fit together?
teacher_understanding.answer: They describe shared public records without unilateral user control and open development using the network's basic features.

items.content:
Find correct statements about RTGS and NEFT: (Pre'25)
1. In RTGS, the settlement time is instantaneous while in case of NEFT, it takes some time.
2. In RTGS, the customer is charged for inward transactions while that is not the case for NEFT.
3. Operating hours for RTGS are restricted on certain days while this is not true for NEFT.
Codes:
items.type_note: The statements form a comparison-based selection question; they must not be treated as three true comparisons.

teacher_understanding.question: Which statements are correct in the question's 2025 context?
teacher_understanding.answer: Statement 1 only; option (a). Statements 2 and 3 are incorrect.

teacher_understanding.question: How do RTGS and NEFT settle transfers?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS means Real Time Gross Settlement: transactions settle individually in real time. NEFT means National Electronic Funds Transfer: transfers are processed through half-hourly batches. 'Instantaneous' describes the RTGS settlement model, not a guarantee that every customer-facing step has zero delay.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does batching distinguish NEFT from RTGS?
teacher_understanding.answer: An RTGS payment does not wait for a batch settlement cycle; an NEFT instruction enters the relevant batch for processing.

teacher_understanding.question: Do inward charges and operating hours differ as statements 2 and 3 claim?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Inward RTGS and NEFT transactions are free to the receiving customer, and both systems operate round the clock on all days in the question's 2025 context.

teacher_understanding.question: How can learners avoid confusing operating hours with settlement mode?
teacher_understanding.answer: Keep separate columns: availability asks when instructions can be processed, while settlement mode asks whether payments settle individually or in batches. Round-the-clock operation does not make NEFT real-time gross settlement.

items.exam_note: Keep the 2025 context: outdated limited-hours facts can lead to a wrong answer. No printed solution.

teacher_understanding.question: Is this the correct selection?
teacher_understanding.answer: Yes. Roman numeral I corresponds to statement 1.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is statement 1 retained?
teacher_understanding.answer: It captures the distinction between real-time individual RTGS settlement and NEFT batch processing.

items.exam_note: Correct by outside explanation.

teacher_understanding.question: Is this combination correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Statement II is incorrect.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is the inward-charge claim wrong?
teacher_understanding.answer: An inward RTGS receipt is free to the receiving customer; the asserted contrast with NEFT is false.

items.exam_note: Inward and outward charges must not be confused.

teacher_understanding.question: Is this combination correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Statement III is incorrect in the 2025 context.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is statement III excluded?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both RTGS and NEFT offer round-the-clock operation on all days, so the claimed restriction on RTGS is outdated.

items.exam_note: Date-sensitive operating-hours trap.

teacher_understanding.question: Is this option correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. It selects the false operating-hours statement and omits the correct settlement statement.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does availability not establish this option?
teacher_understanding.answer: The systems share round-the-clock availability in the question's context, while their settlement mechanisms remain different.

items.exam_note: Reject III and retain I.

items.content:
Find Correct Statement(s) [ Prelims-2018]
1. BHIM app allows the user to transfer money to anyone with a UPI-enabled bank account.
2. While a chip-pin debit card has four factors of authentication, BHIM app has only two factors of authentication.
Answer codes:
items.type_note: The year identifies a PYQ, not a timeline; the comparison is a proposition to evaluate rather than a true factual assertion.

teacher_understanding.question: Which statement is correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: Statement 1 only; option (a). Statement 2's claim of four authentication factors for a chip-pin debit card is incorrect.

teacher_understanding.question: How does BHIM support transfers beyond users of the same app?
teacher_understanding.answer: BHIM uses UPI, the Unified Payments Interface. Transfers work through UPI-enabled bank accounts and the interoperable payment network; the recipient need not use BHIM merely because the sender does.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the authentication comparison be evaluated?
teacher_understanding.answer: A chip-and-PIN debit-card transaction commonly combines possession of the card with knowledge of the PIN. BHIM uses the registered mobile/device linkage and UPI PIN for its payment authentication. Counting screens or steps as separate factors does not make the debit card a four-factor system.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is a factor different from a procedural step?
teacher_understanding.answer: A factor is an independent kind of evidence of identity, such as something possessed or something known. Several steps using the same kind of evidence do not automatically create several distinct factors.

prerequisites: possession and knowledge as authentication factors
items.exam_note: UPSC 2018: do not confuse UPI interoperability with use of the same app, or count steps as factors. No printed key.

teacher_understanding.question: Is this option correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: Yes. The transfer statement is correct and the four-factor comparison is incorrect.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can statement 1 be accepted?
teacher_understanding.answer: BHIM works on interoperable UPI-enabled bank accounts rather than restricting recipients to the sender's app.

items.exam_note: Correct by outside explanation.

teacher_understanding.question: Is this selection correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. It selects the false comparison and excludes the correct transfer statement.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is statement 2 false as a whole?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its four-factor premise for a chip-pin debit card is incorrect, even though it refers to two-factor authentication for BHIM.

items.exam_note: One false clause invalidates a compound statement.

teacher_understanding.question: Is accepting both statements correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Only statement 1 is correct.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must statement 2 be eliminated?
teacher_understanding.answer: Chip-and-PIN authentication does not become four-factor authentication simply because a transaction has multiple steps.

items.exam_note: Reject the numerical authentication trap.

teacher_understanding.question: Is rejecting both statements correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Statement 1 is correct.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should statement 1 not be rejected?
teacher_understanding.answer: UPI allows BHIM users to transfer to UPI-enabled bank accounts across the interoperable network.

items.exam_note: Interoperability preserves statement 1.

1. NPCI helps in promoting the financial inclusion in the country.
items.type_note: The year identifies the source examination, not a timeline. This is an incomplete question continuing onto the next page.

teacher_understanding.question: What proposition is visible, and can the complete answer be chosen here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The visible statement says NPCI helps promote financial inclusion. The rest of the question and its options are not present on this page, so the complete combination cannot be selected from this page alone.

teacher_understanding.question: What does NPCI stand for?
teacher_understanding.answer: NPCI is the National Payments Corporation of India, an organisation associated with India's retail payment infrastructure.

teacher_understanding.question: How can payment infrastructure promote financial inclusion?
teacher_understanding.answer: Interoperable payment services help people use their bank accounts to send and receive money more conveniently. Inclusion involves usable financial services, not merely owning an account.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is 'helps in promoting' an appropriate limited claim?
teacher_understanding.answer: Payment infrastructure supports access and use, but inclusion also depends on factors such as account access, connectivity, affordability and user capability. NPCI does not by itself guarantee universal inclusion.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the visible statement be evaluated?
teacher_understanding.answer: Statement 1 is correct, but choosing a full answer combination requires the continuation.

teacher_understanding.question: Which combination is correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: Option d, 1 and 3 only, in the public, permissionless setting assumed by the question.

teacher_understanding.question: Why reject statement 2?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blockchain can maintain records other than cryptocurrency records; the worked delivery example in i22 shows this distinction.

teacher_understanding.question: How should statements 1 and 3 be qualified?
teacher_understanding.answer: They describe open public participation and development, not unrestricted access to every private network or exemption from law.

replace_items.exam_note: UPSC 2020; no printed answer key. Existing options i6–i9 remain children of this question.

replace_items.content: 1. It is a public ledger that everyone can inspect, but which no single user controls.
replace_items.type_note: The substantive feature is a shared record and distribution of control, not the question's examination date.

teacher_understanding.question: What is a ledger in this context?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a record book maintained electronically. In a public blockchain, participating computers maintain a shared history rather than leaving the authoritative record under one user's unilateral control.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are the records and control located?
teacher_understanding.answer: Copies are maintained across participating network computers. Updates are accepted through the network's validation and agreement rules, rather than merely because one user edits a local copy.

teacher_understanding.question: How can inspection be open while editing is constrained?
teacher_understanding.answer: Reading an entry gives information, not authority. A participant proposing a change must satisfy network rules; changing a private copy does not by itself change the shared accepted history.

teacher_understanding.question: Why use the image of several matching account books?
teacher_understanding.answer: It separates access from control: many people may see the record, but one person's overwritten page is not automatically accepted by everyone else.

replace_items.exam_note: Supports statement 1 and options i6–i9. Public access is not unilateral editing power.

Find correct statements about RTGS and NEFT: (Pre'25)
1. In RTGS, the settlement time is instantaneous while in case of NEFT, it takes some time.
2. In RTGS, the customer is charged for inward transactions while that is not the case for NEFT.
3. Operating hours for RTGS are restricted on certain days while this is not true for NEFT.
Codes:
replace_items.type_note: Question wrapper; typed comparison i23 and settlement process i24 carry the substantive teaching.

teacher_understanding.question: Which option is correct in the 2025 context?
teacher_understanding.answer: Option (a), I only. The inward-charge and restricted-days claims are incorrect.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must availability and settlement mode be separated?
teacher_understanding.answer: Both systems can operate around the clock while processing payments differently: RTGS individually in real time and NEFT through batches.

teacher_understanding.question: How should 'instantaneous' be interpreted?
teacher_understanding.answer: As shorthand for the real-time settlement model, not a promise of zero delay in every customer interface, validation step or account-credit notification.

replace_items.exam_note: Existing options i11–i14 remain unchanged. Solutions are outside; the dated operational explanation is in i23.

replace_items.content:
1. In RTGS, the settlement time is instantaneous while in case of NEFT, it takes some time.
2. In RTGS, the customer is charged for inward transactions while that is not the case for NEFT.
3. Operating hours for RTGS are restricted on certain days while this is not true for NEFT.
replace_items.type_note: Retains the proposed comparison type while evaluating the statements rather than teaching false claims as facts.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the systems compare on settlement, inward charges and availability?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS settles individual payments in real time; NEFT processes transfers in half-hourly batches. Inward receipts are free to receiving customers in both systems. Both operate 24×7 in the question's 2025 setting.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the operative difference behind statement 1?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS does not wait for a batch cycle and settles each payment separately. NEFT groups instructions for batch processing, so a transfer can wait for the relevant cycle.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is 'inward' important?
teacher_understanding.answer: For a receiving merchant, inward means money coming into the account. A possible charge on sending money is a different issue and does not establish a charge on receiving it.

teacher_understanding.question: What dated basis supports rejecting the restricted-hours claim?
teacher_understanding.answer: RBI made NEFT available round the clock from 16 December 2019 and RTGS from 14 December 2020. Both changes precede the question's 2025 context.

replace_items.exam_note: Statement 1 is accepted; statements 2 and 3 are rejected. Date-sensitive facts must be read in the question's context.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a transfer move from the customer to completed interbank settlement?
teacher_understanding.answer: The sender authorises a payment; the sending bank checks and submits it. In RTGS, an accepted payment settles individually through the banks' settlement accounts. In NEFT, instructions enter a batch and participating banks settle the resulting net obligations for that batch. The beneficiary bank then handles credit under the applicable system rules.

teacher_understanding.question: When does each system settle?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS settles individual accepted instructions in real time, subject to system checks and available funds. NEFT settlement follows its half-hourly batch cycles rather than an individual gross settlement for each instruction.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is RTGS called gross settlement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Each payment obligation settles separately at its full value rather than first being combined with other payments to calculate a net amount.

teacher_understanding.question: How is interbank settlement different from an app notification?
teacher_understanding.answer: Settlement completes obligations between participating banks. A customer-facing debit, beneficiary credit and notification are related stages, but their display times are not themselves the definition of settlement.

replace_items.exam_note: Distinguish bank-level settlement from customer display speed and from system availability.

unpack.consequence: The same customer amount can travel through different settlement mechanisms; it does not imply creation of new customer money.

unpack.level_extra: The chosen ₹2,00,000 example is suitable for illustrating RTGS; compare alternatives, not two payments made together.

real_world_example.place: shop and two Indian banks; hypothetical alternative scenarios

steps.step: The buyer authorises ₹2,00,000 for stock and the sending bank checks the instruction.
steps.mechanism_link: Customer authorisation initiates the transfer; it is not by itself completed interbank settlement.

steps.step: Under the RTGS alternative, the accepted ₹2,00,000 obligation settles individually in full.
steps.mechanism_link: Real-time gross settlement avoids waiting for a batch.

teacher_understanding.question: Which option is correct?
teacher_understanding.answer: Option (a), 1 only. The UPI transfer statement is correct; the four-factor premise for chip-and-PIN cards is incorrect.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the recipient use a different app?
teacher_understanding.answer: BHIM uses interoperable UPI-enabled bank accounts, so common payment infrastructure rather than identical app choice connects sender and recipient.

replace_items.type_note: The substantive content is an interoperable account-to-account transfer mechanism.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a hypothetical ₹500 BHIM payment reach a merchant using another UPI app?
teacher_understanding.answer: The payer identifies the merchant's linked UPI account, checks the payee and amount, and authorises the payment using the UPI PIN on the registered device. The payment network and banks process the instruction; on successful completion the payer's balance falls by ₹500 and the merchant's rises by ₹500.

teacher_understanding.question: When should the customer treat the payment as successful?
teacher_understanding.answer: After the transaction is successfully processed and its status and receipt are confirmed, not merely after entering an amount or opening an app.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is using the same app unnecessary?
teacher_understanding.answer: UPI provides interoperable payment connections between participating bank accounts; BHIM is an interface to that infrastructure, not a closed recipient list.

teacher_understanding.question: How do possession and knowledge enter this sequence?
teacher_understanding.answer: The registered mobile/device linkage supplies possession-related evidence; entering the UPI PIN supplies knowledge-related evidence. Selecting a recipient and checking the amount are steps, not additional independent factors.

replace_items.exam_note: Supports statement 1; recipient need not use BHIM simply because the sender does.

teacher_understanding.question: What follows for the idea that every Post Office product belongs in M4?

items.content: 1. It is a public ledger that everyone can inspect, but which no single user controls.
items.type_note: The substantive feature is a shared record and distribution of control, not the question's examination date.

teacher_understanding.question: What is a ledger in this context?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is a record book maintained electronically. In a public blockchain, participating computers maintain a shared history rather than leaving the authoritative record under one user's unilateral control.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are the records and control located?
teacher_understanding.answer: Copies are maintained across participating network computers. Updates are accepted through the network's validation and agreement rules, rather than merely because one user edits a local copy.

teacher_understanding.question: How can inspection be open while editing is constrained?
teacher_understanding.answer: Reading an entry gives information, not authority. A participant proposing a change must satisfy network rules; changing a private copy does not by itself change the shared accepted history.

teacher_understanding.question: Why use the image of several matching account books?
teacher_understanding.answer: It separates access from control: many people may see the record, but one person's overwritten page is not automatically accepted by everyone else.

items.exam_note: Supports statement 1 and options i6–i9. Public access is not unilateral editing power.

why_chain.step: Parties sharing a record need a way to resist one party's unilateral alteration.
Shared copies and agreed validation rules separate proposed entries from accepted history.

unpack.example_or_place: Hypothetical mandi delivery ledger: seller and buyer can inspect the same accepted delivery record.
unpack.consequence: Transparency concerns who can read; shared control concerns how an accepted record can be changed.
unpack.visual_verb: replicate the accepted entry and reject a unilateral overwrite
unpack.level_extra: This explains the question's public blockchain model; permissioned networks can restrict participation.

2. Structure and design of blockchain is such that all the data in it are about cryptocurrency only.
3. Applications that use basic features of blockchain can be developed without anybody’s permission.
items.type_note: These propositions are opened through a worked application and record-validation sequence; statement 2 remains a false proposition, not a taught fact.

teacher_understanding.question: How could a non-cryptocurrency record be proposed and accepted?
teacher_understanding.answer: In a hypothetical delivery application, a seller submits a signed record saying 10 onion sacks were delivered to a buyer. Participating validators check the required authorisation and record format and apply network agreement rules before the entry becomes part of the accepted shared history.

teacher_understanding.question: When does the proposal become a shared accepted record?
teacher_understanding.answer: After the required validation and agreement steps, not simply when the seller types it or a viewer reads it.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does this example refute 'cryptocurrency only'?
teacher_understanding.answer: The recorded subject is delivery of onions. The method of sharing and validating records does not require the subject of every entry to be cryptocurrency.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the example show both the power and limits of validation?
teacher_understanding.answer: A viewer cannot replace the accepted quantity with 20 merely by editing a screen. Yet network validation alone does not prove that 10 physical sacks actually arrived: reliable reporting or verification of the real event is still needed.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does permissionless development not mean permissionless conduct?
teacher_understanding.answer: Open network features can be used to build applications without a central owner's approval, but legal duties and the application's own access requirements may still apply.

items.exam_note: Supports selection of statements 1 and 3, and rejection of statement 2; options i6–i9.

why_chain.step: A seller and buyer need a common delivery history without one party silently rewriting it.

unpack.consequence: Separate the record-keeping technology from the goods or claims recorded.
unpack.visual_verb: submit, validate, replicate, and block an unauthorised overwrite
unpack.level_extra: Validation of an authorised report is not automatic proof of its physical-world truth.

real_world_example.place: hypothetical mandi using a public blockchain delivery application

steps.step: The seller submits an authorised delivery record for 10 sacks, with the buyer's confirmation where the application's rules require it.
steps.mechanism_link: A real-goods event becomes a proposed digital record.

steps.step: Validators check the required authorisation and rules; network agreement adds the entry to shared history.
steps.mechanism_link: Rule-based acceptance, not one user's command, determines the shared entry.

steps.step: A viewer reads the record but cannot make an unsupported local change to 20 sacks become the network's accepted history.
steps.mechanism_link: Inspection does not confer unilateral editing control.

real_world_example.term_after: This illustrates a blockchain application for delivery records rather than cryptocurrency-only data.

items.content:
1. In RTGS, the settlement time is instantaneous while in case of NEFT, it takes some time.
2. In RTGS, the customer is charged for inward transactions while that is not the case for NEFT.
3. Operating hours for RTGS are restricted on certain days while this is not true for NEFT.
items.type_note: Retains the proposed comparison type while evaluating the statements rather than teaching false claims as facts.

teacher_understanding.question: How do the systems compare on settlement, inward charges and availability?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS settles individual payments in real time; NEFT processes transfers in half-hourly batches. Inward receipts are free to receiving customers in both systems. Both operate 24×7 in the question's 2025 setting.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the operative difference behind statement 1?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS does not wait for a batch cycle and settles each payment separately. NEFT groups instructions for batch processing, so a transfer can wait for the relevant cycle.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is 'inward' important?
teacher_understanding.answer: For a receiving merchant, inward means money coming into the account. A possible charge on sending money is a different issue and does not establish a charge on receiving it.

teacher_understanding.question: What dated basis supports rejecting the restricted-hours claim?
teacher_understanding.answer: RBI made NEFT available round the clock from 16 December 2019 and RTGS from 14 December 2020. Both changes precede the question's 2025 context.

items.exam_note: Statement 1 is accepted; statements 2 and 3 are rejected. Date-sensitive facts must be read in the question's context.

items.content: 1. In RTGS, the settlement time is instantaneous while in case of NEFT, it takes some time.
items.type_note: A separate process item opens the mechanism underlying the printed comparison.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a transfer move from the customer to completed interbank settlement?
teacher_understanding.answer: The sender authorises a payment; the sending bank checks and submits it. In RTGS, an accepted payment settles individually through the banks' settlement accounts. In NEFT, instructions enter a batch and participating banks settle the resulting net obligations for that batch. The beneficiary bank then handles credit under the applicable system rules.

teacher_understanding.question: When does each system settle?
teacher_understanding.answer: RTGS settles individual accepted instructions in real time, subject to system checks and available funds. NEFT settlement follows its half-hourly batch cycles rather than an individual gross settlement for each instruction.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is RTGS called gross settlement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Each payment obligation settles separately at its full value rather than first being combined with other payments to calculate a net amount.

teacher_understanding.question: How is interbank settlement different from an app notification?
teacher_understanding.answer: Settlement completes obligations between participating banks. A customer-facing debit, beneficiary credit and notification are related stages, but their display times are not themselves the definition of settlement.

items.exam_note: Distinguish bank-level settlement from customer display speed and from system availability.

terms.plain_meaning: हर भुगतान की पूरी रकम का अलग निपटारा
terms.everyday_image: दो बिलों को काटकर बची रकम देने के बजाय हर बिल अलग चुकाना।

terms.plain_meaning: एक तय दौर में साथ लिए गए कई निर्देश
terms.everyday_image: कूरियर की अगली खेप में कई पार्सल साथ जाना।

why_chain.step: A buyer and supplier at different banks need both the customer transfer and the banks' obligations completed.
RTGS completes individual gross obligations; NEFT uses batch processing and net settlement.

unpack.example_or_place: Hypothetical ₹2,00,000 payment for shop stock, compared under two alternative transfer methods.
unpack.consequence: The same customer amount can travel through different settlement mechanisms; it does not imply creation of new customer money.
unpack.visual_verb: send one payment directly versus queue instructions into a batch
unpack.level_extra: The chosen ₹2,00,000 example is suitable for illustrating RTGS; compare alternatives, not two payments made together.

real_world_example.place: shop and two Indian banks; hypothetical alternative scenarios

steps.step: The buyer authorises ₹2,00,000 for stock and the sending bank checks the instruction.
steps.mechanism_link: Customer authorisation initiates the transfer; it is not by itself completed interbank settlement.

steps.step: Under the RTGS alternative, the accepted ₹2,00,000 obligation settles individually in full.
steps.mechanism_link: Real-time gross settlement avoids waiting for a batch.

steps.step: Under the NEFT alternative, the same instruction enters a batch whose bank-level net obligations settle before the receiving bank completes the relevant credit steps.
steps.mechanism_link: Batch processing differs from individual gross settlement even if the customer balances eventually change by the same amount.

real_world_example.term_after: These alternatives illustrate RTGS and NEFT settlement.
real_world_example.real_life_link: A business paying a supplier must distinguish submission, bank settlement, beneficiary credit and notification.

items.content: 1. BHIM app allows the user to transfer money to anyone with a UPI-enabled bank account.
items.type_note: The substantive content is an interoperable account-to-account transfer mechanism.

teacher_understanding.question: How does a hypothetical ₹500 BHIM payment reach a merchant using another UPI app?
teacher_understanding.answer: The payer identifies the merchant's linked UPI account, checks the payee and amount, and authorises the payment using the UPI PIN on the registered device. The payment network and banks process the instruction; on successful completion the payer's balance falls by ₹500 and the merchant's rises by ₹500.

teacher_understanding.question: When should the customer treat the payment as successful?
teacher_understanding.answer: After the transaction is successfully processed and its status and receipt are confirmed, not merely after entering an amount or opening an app.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is using the same app unnecessary?
teacher_understanding.answer: UPI provides interoperable payment connections between participating bank accounts; BHIM is an interface to that infrastructure, not a closed recipient list.

teacher_understanding.question: How do possession and knowledge enter this sequence?
teacher_understanding.answer: The registered mobile/device linkage supplies possession-related evidence; entering the UPI PIN supplies knowledge-related evidence. Selecting a recipient and checking the amount are steps, not additional independent factors.

items.exam_note: Supports statement 1; recipient need not use BHIM simply because the sender does.

terms.plain_meaning: ऐसा बैंक खाता जो UPI से पैसे भेजने या पाने के लिए जुड़ा हो
terms.everyday_image: अलग बैंकों के खाते एक साझा भुगतान रास्ते से जुड़ना।

terms.plain_meaning: UPI के रास्ते भुगतान करने की app
terms.everyday_image: रास्ता साझा है, उस पर जाने के लिए चुना गया दरवाजा BHIM है।

why_chain.step: A shopper needs to pay a merchant without matching the merchant's app or bank.
UPI interoperability connects eligible accounts while authentication authorises the debit.

unpack.example_or_place: Hypothetical ₹500 grocery payment using BHIM to a merchant using another UPI app.
unpack.consequence: Interoperability widens whom a user can pay; authentication protects permission to debit the account.
unpack.visual_verb: verify the payee, authorise, debit one account and credit the other
unpack.level_extra: UPI means Unified Payments Interface; app, bank account and payment network are different layers.

steps.step: The shopper identifies the merchant's UPI-linked account and verifies a ₹500 payment.
steps.mechanism_link: Interoperability identifies a reachable account without requiring the same app.

steps.step: On the registered device, the shopper enters the UPI PIN to authorise the instruction.
steps.mechanism_link: Possession-related linkage and PIN knowledge authorise the debit.

steps.step: After successful processing, the shopper's balance becomes ₹1,500 and the merchant's ₹3,500.
steps.mechanism_link: Account-to-account transfer moves existing money; it does not create ₹500.

real_world_example.term_after: This is an interoperable UPI transfer initiated through BHIM.
real_world_example.real_life_link: The page's statement concerns paying across UPI-enabled accounts, as in a household purchase.

items.content: 2. While a chip-pin debit card has four factors of authentication, BHIM app has only two factors of authentication.
items.type_note: Retains the proposed comparison type but explicitly rejects the printed four-factor proposition.

teacher_understanding.question: How do chip-and-PIN cards and BHIM compare in the question's authentication model?
teacher_understanding.answer: A chip-and-PIN card combines possession of the card with knowledge of its PIN. BHIM combines registered mobile/device linkage with knowledge of the UPI PIN. The statement's claim of four factors for the debit card is incorrect.

teacher_understanding.question: What differs, and what is shared?
teacher_understanding.answer: The possession-related object differs: card versus registered mobile/device arrangement. Both use a secret PIN as knowledge-related evidence in the transactions being compared.

teacher_understanding.question: Why are four screens not four factors?
teacher_understanding.answer: Opening an app, choosing a payee, entering an amount and confirming a screen are actions. They do not independently establish four different kinds of identity evidence.

teacher_understanding.question: How does an everyday lock image help?
teacher_understanding.answer: Having a key and knowing a secret code are different kinds of proof. Turning the same key through several steps does not create several independent kinds of proof.

items.exam_note: Supports rejection of statement 2 and options i17–i18; do not count interface actions as factors.

items.content: 1. NPCI helps in promoting the financial inclusion in the country.
items.type_note: The substantive claim links payment infrastructure to improved financial access and use, rather than describing a timeline.

teacher_understanding.question: What does NPCI stand for?
teacher_understanding.answer: NPCI is the National Payments Corporation of India, associated with India's retail payment infrastructure.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can payment infrastructure help financial inclusion?
teacher_understanding.answer: An account is more useful when a household can receive and make payments conveniently. Interoperable infrastructure reduces the need for sender and recipient to use the same bank or app, supporting actual use rather than merely account ownership.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the hypothetical household example show the mechanism?
teacher_understanding.answer: A worker sends ₹1,000 from a participating account to a family member's linked account. The family member receives usable funds without requiring a same-bank arrangement; the sender's balance falls and the recipient's rises by the same amount.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the example establish, and what does it not establish?
teacher_understanding.answer: It illustrates a route from interoperable infrastructure to convenient account use. It neither measures inclusion gains nor proves that everyone has the devices, connectivity or ability needed to use that route.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the scope of the claim actually printed?
teacher_understanding.answer: The statement says NPCI 'helps in promoting' financial inclusion; it does not provide a numerical measure or claim that NPCI alone achieves it.

items.exam_note: Evaluates visible statement 1 of the incomplete 2017 question; infrastructure is an enabling contributor, not a sufficient condition.

terms.plain_meaning: लोगों तक काम की financial सेवाएँ पहुँचना और उनका इस्तेमाल कर पाना
terms.everyday_image: सिर्फ पासबुक होना नहीं, जरूरत पर खाते से पैसे भेज और पा सकना।

terms.plain_meaning: National Payments Corporation of India; साझा retail payment व्यवस्था से जुड़ी संस्था
terms.everyday_image: अलग बैंकों के बीच भुगतान का साझा रास्ता बनाने वाली व्यवस्था।

why_chain.step: A worker's household needs money that can be received and used without an unnecessary same-bank barrier.
Interoperable payment infrastructure makes eligible accounts more usable and can therefore support inclusion.

unpack.example_or_place: Hypothetical worker sending household money to a family member through interoperable payments.
unpack.consequence: Usable access improves in the illustration, but infrastructure alone does not establish universal or measured inclusion.
unpack.visual_verb: bridge two banks and move funds into usable household access
unpack.level_extra: Distinguish a causal illustration from evidence of a measured policy outcome.

real_world_example.place: worker's town and family member's village; hypothetical

steps.step: Assume both people have the required access and linked accounts; the worker authorises ₹1,000 across participating banks.
steps.mechanism_link: Interoperability removes a same-bank requirement for this payment.

steps.step: The successful transfer lowers the worker's balance to ₹2,000 and raises the family member's to ₹1,200.
steps.mechanism_link: Account infrastructure becomes a usable channel for receiving household funds.

steps.step: The family member can use the received money for household needs through available payment or withdrawal facilities.
steps.mechanism_link: Practical use, not merely possession of an account, is the inclusion-related outcome illustrated.

real_world_example.term_after: This illustrates how payment infrastructure can help promote financial inclusion.
real_world_example.real_life_link: Families sending money home encounter the need for usable accounts; this hypothetical example is not a measured estimate of NPCI's inclusion impact.
